title: A kingdom, or a word?
hookLine: Bhima argues for artha, wealth and power, and Yudhishthira answers that dharma comes first: he gave his word
tomorrow: who walks into a stuck camp with a plan?

lines: THE BROTHER WHO GAVE HIS WORD.
cards: Bhima has been listening, and he's done waiting. He's built for action, strong and impatient. He's watched his brothers live on roots and his wife sleep on the ground, and he can't see the point.
Our enemies cheated, he says. Why are we keeping faith with cheats? Let's go back and take what's ours.
It's a fair question, and he asks it loudly.

teach.b: Bhima's case is strong, and the epic lets him make it in full. The game was a trap. Every day in the forest, their enemies grow stronger.

And he argues from the tradition itself. A life, he says, has aims: dharma, doing right; artha, wealth and power; kama, love and pleasure. You've held on to dharma alone, brother, and let the others starve.
Yudhishthira hears him out, then answers with one thing.

I gave my word. In the hall, in front of everyone, he agreed to the terms: the years in the forest, then a year in hiding. Breaking that promise now, he says, would be worse to him than losing the kingdom.
The old word for what he's holding is satya: being someone whose word holds. Then he adds something practical: look who stands on the other side. Bhishma, Drona, Karna.
We aren't ready. Here's the teaching.

Hindu thought names the aims of a human life, the purusharthas: dharma, artha and kama, and later a fourth, moksha, release. None of them is shameful. Wanting success, money, a win: that's artha, an honored aim.
But dharma comes first, and holds the others in shape. A kingdom taken by breaking your word would be artha without dharma. Bhima isn't wrong to want the kingdom back, and the epic doesn't mock him.
Yudhishthira just won't buy it at that price.

how: Yudhishthira's insistence on keeping his word in exile is held up in Hindu storytelling as a picture of satya, truthfulness, and Bhima's speech on dharma, artha and kama is one of the epic's classic discussions of the aims of life.

o: the kingdom the brothers mean to win back
the forest where the brothers wait out their promise
the war camp where the brothers train to fight

games.q: two brothers in the forest — tap the pairs.
p: you've let artha and kama starve
I gave my word in the hall
wealth and power, an honored aim

s: Yudhishthira refused to fight only because he was afraid
his first reason was the word he gave; he also judged honestly that they weren't ready.
Bhima argued from the aims of life: dharma, artha and kama
he told Yudhishthira he'd held to dharma alone and let the others starve.
in Hindu teaching, wanting wealth and success is shameful
artha is one of the honored aims of life; the teaching is that dharma leads it.

games.q: you're Yudhishthira. Bhima says you've chased dharma and starved artha, so take the kingdom back now. what do you answer?
o: agree: a promise to cheats doesn't bind.
keep the word you gave: artha matters, but dharma leads.
games.why: he keeps it. breaking his word, he says, would be worse than losing the kingdom. artha is a real aim, but it moves inside dharma.

practice: Think of something you want right now: a win, a raise, a grade, a place. It's allowed; artha is an honored aim. Now think of a promise that stands in its way.

Let the Bhima in you ask, why not drop it, and breathe; then let the Yudhishthira in you ask, who would I be if I did, and breathe again. If you pray, offer both the wanting and the promise; if not, just hold them side by side.

wordCard.voice: Vana. The forest of exile, where Bhima argues for artha and Yudhishthira keeps the word he gave in the hall.

orig.note: Sanskrit satya: truth, and truthfulness, being someone whose word holds.

carryVoice: Your line: artha matters, but dharma leads. For Yudhishthira, a word that held was worth more than a kingdom. Tomorrow: who walks into a stuck camp with a plan? Day seven hundred eighty, done.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Aranyaka Parva), Bhima's appeal to Yudhishthira on dharma, artha and kama, and Yudhishthira's reply (the promise made at the dice game; the strength of Bhishma, Drona and Karna)
